promptText: What is a model card, and why would an engineer bother writing one?
options: A model card is internal source-code documentation intended only for the original engineering team

A model card is a structured document attached to a specific model version describing intended use, what it should not be used for, training/grounding data, evaluation results, and known limitations, so people who did not build the system can assess whether it is safe to use
A model card is a legal contract between the company and the model provider
A model card is only required for models that will never reach production
explanation: A model card is written for non-authors — auditors, downstream consumers, incident responders, risk committees — to evaluate a model's fitness and limitations without needing to read its implementation.

promptText: What is the difference between a code review and a model governance review?
options: They are the same process performed by different job titles

A code review checks whether the implementation is correct and maintainable; a governance review checks whether the system is approved to exist for its intended purpose at all — risk tier, accountable ownership, data lineage — independently of code quality, so a system can pass one and still be blocked by the other
Governance review only applies after a system has already failed code review
Code review is mandatory only for AI systems, while governance review applies to all software
explanation: These are orthogonal checks: code review evaluates engineering quality, while governance review evaluates whether the organization has decided the system is permitted to run at all, given its risk and accountability profile.

promptText: In the 'three lines of defense' model, where does a typical Java/Spring application engineering team sit, and what is its core obligation?
options: The third line (internal audit), responsible for auditing the second line's policies

The first line — the team building and operating the system day-to-day — whose job is to build systems that make lineage, ownership, and approval status checkable by the second and third lines, not to self-certify their own compliance
The second line, responsible for setting company-wide risk policy
Engineering teams sit outside all three lines since the model applies only to compliance staff
explanation: The first line owns risk day-to-day and builds the system; the second line (risk/compliance) independently reviews and approves; the third line (audit) verifies the first two actually followed the process — engineering teams are almost always the first line.

promptText: What are the four core functions of the NIST AI Risk Management Framework (AI RMF)?
options: Build, Test, Deploy, Monitor
Govern, Map, Measure, Manage — with Govern treated as the foundation the other three operate within, rather than a sequential first step
Plan, Do, Check, Act
Approve, Deploy, Retire, Archive
explanation: NIST AI RMF organizes risk management around Govern (culture, policy, accountability), Map (context and risk framing), Measure (quantitative/qualitative risk assessment), and Manage (resource allocation, monitoring, response) — with Govern underpinning the other three.

promptText: What is 'shadow AI,' and why is it specifically a governance problem?
options: Shadow AI refers to AI models that intentionally hide their reasoning steps from users

Shadow AI is AI usage that exists outside an organization's official inventory and governance process (e.g., a team wiring in a third-party LLM API unreviewed); it is a governance problem because it is invisible to risk tiering, data-handling review, and vendor assessment, representing unmanaged risk that surfaces only after something goes wrong
Shadow AI is a synonym for any AI model that underperforms its benchmark
Shadow AI only refers to AI systems used exclusively at night outside business hours
explanation: Governance controls can only be applied to systems governance knows exist; shadow AI bypasses intake entirely, leaving risk unmeasured and unmanaged until an incident forces discovery.

promptText: Why does an organization need an AI system inventory (distinct from a technical model registry)?
options: An inventory is only useful for calculating cloud infrastructure costs

Governance, legal, and risk functions cannot manage what they cannot see — without an inventory there is no way to answer questions like which systems process personal data through a third party, or to demonstrate to a regulator that AI risk is actually being managed rather than merely claimed
An inventory replaces the need for any model card or documentation
An inventory is required only for models trained entirely in-house, not for third-party APIs
explanation: An organization-wide inventory of AI systems, their purpose, owner, and risk tier is the visibility layer that makes every other governance activity (tiering, review, audit response) possible in the first place.

promptText: Why should a model registry gate deployments on prompt template version, not just model version?
options: Prompt versions are purely cosmetic and never affect model behavior, so this is unnecessary in practice

A prompt-only change can materially change a model's behavior even when the underlying model is unchanged; gating only on model version leaves prompt changes completely outside governance visibility, creating a real gap where an unreviewed prompt reaches production under an already-approved model
Gating on prompt version is only relevant for open-source models, never for hosted provider APIs
Model version and prompt version are always changed together, so tracking one implies the other
explanation: Because prompt edits can change behavior as significantly as a model swap, mature governance frameworks require re-approval for prompt-only changes above minimal risk; many real programs miss this by gating solely on model version.

promptText: The chapter models AI risk informally as Severity x Likelihood x Scale / Reversibility. What does this explain about why a hallucination in an internal five-employee tool is tiered far below the same hallucination rate in a customer-facing system serving millions?
options: Internal tools are exempt from governance by definition, regardless of risk

The formula's Scale term (number of people affected) differs enormously between the two cases, so even identical Severity and Likelihood produce very different overall risk, justifying proportionally different review rigor
Severity is always zero for internal tools, making the comparison meaningless
The formula only applies to systems that are fully autonomous with no human review
explanation: The same failure rate multiplied by a vastly different number of affected people produces very different expected harm, which is why intake questionnaires implicitly probe scale alongside severity, likelihood, and reversibility rather than treating any single factor in isolation.

promptText: What is the core distinction between AI governance and MLOps?
options: MLOps and AI governance are the same discipline with different marketing names

MLOps is the engineering discipline for building, deploying, monitoring, and retraining models reliably — 'how do we ship and operate this well'; AI governance is the organizational discipline deciding whether a system should exist, who is accountable, and what risk it may carry, verified independently of the building team — 'should this system exist, and how do we know'
MLOps only applies to training pipelines, while governance only applies to inference pipelines
Governance is a subset of MLOps focused exclusively on model versioning
explanation: The two are complementary: governance relies on MLOps capabilities (versioning, monitoring, reproducibility) as the technical substrate that makes its claims verifiable, while MLOps without governance can ship excellent systems nobody has assessed for organizational risk.

promptText: Why is a risk-based governance program generally preferred over a rule-based one that applies an identical fixed checklist to every AI system?
options: Rule-based programs are always faster to implement and equally effective at scale

A rule-based program either becomes an unsustainable bottleneck applied uniformly or gets quietly ignored as AI adoption grows, while a risk-based program calibrates requirements to the assessed risk of each use case, keeping rigor proportional to actual stakes and staying viable as volume increases
Risk-based programs cannot be audited, unlike rule-based programs
Rule-based programs are required by every AI regulation, making risk-based programs illegal
explanation: Uniform maximum rigor either overwhelms low-stakes work or gets bypassed under deadline pressure; risk-based tiering concentrates scarce review capacity where it actually reduces material risk, which is why most mature programs adopt it.

promptText: Why must a governance deployment gate include a documented, logged emergency-override path rather than being a hard, unconditional block?
options: Emergency overrides are only needed for non-production environments

A gate with no escape hatch invites people to route around it entirely outside the system during a genuine incident, which is worse than a governed override; the fix is a logged, reviewed override path, not the absence of a gate
Overrides eliminate the need for any audit logging at all
Emergency overrides should never require after-the-fact review since speed matters more than accountability during an incident
explanation: An inflexible gate creates pressure to bypass governance entirely during a real incident; a documented, logged override with mandatory after-the-fact review preserves both responsiveness and accountability.

promptText: In the Spring AI GovernanceAdvisor pattern (checking registry status before allowing a ChatClient call), what deliberate separation of concerns does the advisor maintain?
options: The advisor decides governance policy itself, inventing approval rules inline based on request content

The advisor enforces a decision already recorded in the registry — it does not decide policy — mirroring how an authorization filter checks a permission the security team defined rather than inventing authorization rules inline
The advisor bypasses the registry entirely and relies only on hard-coded risk tiers in the source code
The advisor's only responsibility is formatting error messages for end users
explanation: The advisor's job is enforcement, not policy-making: it looks up the registry's recorded approval status and blocks or allows the call accordingly, keeping the same clean separation used for authorization checks against externally defined permissions.

promptText: Another team is discovered to have quietly integrated a third-party LLM API into a customer-facing feature without going through AI governance intake. What is the correct staff-level response sequence?
options: Immediately shut down the feature and publicly reprimand the team as the first and only action

First assess actual risk exposure (what data reaches the third party, what decisions the output influences) rather than treating it purely as a process violation, retroactively bring it through intake if risk is low, and separately fix the underlying incentive by pairing technical detection (egress monitoring, billing anomaly alerts) with making the sanctioned path easier to use than the workaround
Ignore the discovery since the feature is already live and rolling it back would be disruptive
Require the team to rewrite the feature from scratch using a different programming language as a penalty
explanation: A staff-level response prioritizes actual risk assessment over reflexive punishment, retroactively governs low-risk cases, and treats the root cause as a systems-design problem — making the compliant path the path of least resistance — rather than relying solely on after-the-fact enforcement.

promptText: A product leader argues mandatory governance review is slowing a competitive fast-follow launch and should be relaxed. What is the strongest response from the engineer accountable for the platform?
options: Immediately agree to skip governance review entirely to preserve the launch timeline

Reframe around risk-proportionate process rather than a binary on/off choice: confirm the actual risk tier, show that a genuinely low-risk tier's process is already fast (the slowness may indicate mis-tiering), make tradeoffs explicit in business terms if the use case is genuinely high risk, and offer to accelerate the review itself (pre-built evaluation harnesses, a fast lane) rather than removing it
Escalate to the CEO to have the product leader's authority over launches revoked
Refuse to discuss the matter further since governance policy cannot be questioned by product leadership
explanation: The correct move separates the complaint (perceived slowness) from the actual lever (mis-tiering or a slow review process), makes the business risk explicit if the use case is genuinely high-risk, and offers to fix the bottleneck (faster review tooling) rather than removing the safeguard.

promptText: How should a model registry and deployment gate be designed so governance is enforced structurally rather than relying on teams voluntarily following policy?
options: Publish a policy document and trust engineers to read and follow it before every deployment

Have the CI/CD pipeline itself query the registry before promoting any artifact and refuse to deploy anything not marked approved for that exact environment; wrap every application-level model call with an advisor that independently re-checks status and writes an immutable audit entry; make approval status changes append-only and tied to strong authentication; auto-revert status to 'in review' when a revalidation date passes; and provide a logged, time-boxed emergency-override path requiring mandatory after-the-fact review
Rely solely on a quarterly manual audit to catch any ungoverned deployments after the fact
Require every engineer to manually email the risk committee before each deploy with no technical enforcement
explanation: Structural enforcement means bypassing governance requires bypassing the deployment pipeline itself, not just skipping a form — combining a pipeline-level gate, a runtime advisor check with audit logging, append-only approval history, automatic revalidation expiry, and a logged override path closes the gaps a purely policy-based program leaves open.
